payload.markdown:
Your final is Wednesday 9am, and last year's paper asks you to trace heaps by hand. The good news: a heap is the simplest tree there is, because it lives inside a flat array. The shape property from slide 4 of Lecture 4 says the tree is complete — every level full except the last, which fills from the left — and that shape is exactly what the array indices encode. The heap property (min-heap: every parent ≤ its children) is what lets you find the minimum instantly at index 0.

You already traced hash tables bucket by bucket; a heap trace is the same kind of mechanical work, but the rule is even stricter: after every insert or extract-min, the array must still be a complete tree with the heap property. Two operations do all the work — sift-up for insert (slide 6) and sift-down for extract-min (slide 8). Master those two loops and the whole node is yours.

The trap this node exists to prevent: treating build-heap as n inserts. Slide 10 shows the bottom-up method (Floyd, 1964) that runs in O(n), and the exam's Q3e asks you to explain the difference. You will trace it, then build it, then explain it.

payload.intro: Trace insert and extract-min on the exact arrays from your slides, then run Floyd's build-heap. Do each step on paper; the array after each step is what the exam wants.

steps.title: Insert 2 into [1, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8] (min-heap)
steps.detail_markdown: Push 2 to the end: index 6. Its parent is index 2 (value 6). 2 < 6, so swap → [1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8, 6]. Now at index 2; parent is index 0 (value 1). 2 > 1, stop.
steps.warning: Forgetting to compare with the parent after the swap — you must move up one level each time.
steps.check: Array is [1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8, 6]; every parent ≤ its children.

steps.title: Extract-min from [1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8, 6]
steps.detail_markdown: Save root 1. Pop the last element (6) and put it at index 0 → [6, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8]. Sift down: children of index 0 are 3 and 2; the smaller is 2, swap → [2, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8]. Index 2 has one child, 8; 6 < 8, stop.
steps.warning: Swapping with the larger child instead of the smaller — always pick the smaller child in a min-heap.
steps.check: Final array [2, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8]; the minimum 2 is at the root.

steps.title: Build a min-heap from [9, 4, 7, 1, 2, 6] bottom-up
steps.detail_markdown: n = 6, so start at index ⌊6/2⌋−1 = 2. Sift-down at index 2: children 5 and 6 (values 2 and 6); smaller is 2, swap → [9, 4, 6, 1, 2, 7]. Next index 1: children 3 and 4 (values 1 and 2); smaller is 1, swap → [9, 1, 6, 4, 2, 7]. Next index 0: children 1 and 2 (values 1 and 6); smaller is 1, swap → [1, 9, 6, 4, 2, 7]; sift down again: children of index 1 are 3 and 4 (values 4 and 2); smaller is 2, swap → [1, 2, 6, 4, 9, 7].
steps.warning: Skipping the second sift-down after the root swap — the new root may need to travel more than one level.

steps.title: Heapsort: build a max-heap, then extract n−1 times
steps.detail_markdown: Build a max-heap (same bottom-up, but sift up the larger child). Then repeat n−1 times: swap root with the last element, shrink the heap by one, sift-down the new root. Each extraction puts the current maximum at the end, so the array sorts in place.
steps.warning: Forgetting to shrink the heap after each swap — the sorted tail must never be sifted again.
steps.check: After n−1 extractions the array is sorted ascending.

payload.title: Heap trace checklist

items.text: Array is complete: no gaps before the last level
items.why: The shape property must hold after every operation.
The heap property is what makes find-min O(1).

items.text: Insert: new key placed at the end, then sifted up
items.why: Adding at the end preserves the shape; sifting restores the heap property.

items.text: Extract-min: last element moved to root, then sifted down
items.why: Moving the last leaf keeps the tree complete; sifting down restores order.

items.text: Sift-down always swaps with the smaller child (min-heap)
items.why: Swapping with the larger child would violate the heap property.

items.text: Build-heap starts at index ⌊n/2⌋−1 and goes down to 0
items.why: Leaves are already heaps; only internal nodes need sifting.

items.text: Heapsort swaps root with last, shrinks heap, sifts down
items.why: Each extraction places the max at the end, sorting in place.

payload.note: Keep this open while you trace; tick each line only when the array on your paper satisfies it.

payload.title: Build-heap trace on [9, 4, 7, 1, 2, 6]
payload.markdown:
Slide 10 shows the steps; here is the full working.

n = 6, so the first internal node is at index ⌊6/2⌋−1 = 2.

- i = 2 (value 7): children at 5 and 6 are 2 and 6; smaller is 2 → swap → [9, 4, 6, 1, 2, 7]
- i = 1 (value 4): children at 3 and 4 are 1 and 2; smaller is 1 → swap → [9, 1, 6, 4, 2, 7]
- i = 0 (value 9): children at 1 and 2 are 1 and 6; smaller is 1 → swap → [1, 9, 6, 4, 2, 7]; now sift down from index 1: children at 3 and 4 are 4 and 2; smaller is 2 → swap → [1, 2, 6, 4, 9, 7]

Final min-heap: [1, 2, 6, 4, 9, 7]. Each parent ≤ its children: 1 ≤ 2, 1 ≤ 6, 2 ≤ 4, 2 ≤ 9, 6 ≤ 7.

payload.instructions_markdown: Write the `insert` function for a min-heap stored as an array. It takes the current heap array and a value x, pushes x to the end, and sifts it up until the heap property holds. Mutate the array in place; the function does not need to return anything. Example: `insert([1, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8], 2)` should leave the array as `[1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8, 6]`.
hints: Push x to the end, then set i to the last index.
While i > 0, compare with parent at Math.floor((i-1)/2).
If parent is greater, swap and move i to the parent; otherwise stop.

assessments.prompt: Explain why building a heap bottom-up from n unordered keys takes O(n) time, while inserting the n keys one at a time takes O(n log n) time in the worst case.

answer_key.reference_answer: Bottom-up build sifts down each internal node; the sum of all node heights in a complete tree is O(n), so the total work is O(n). Repeated inserts each sift up O(log n) levels, so n inserts cost O(n log n) in the worst case.

rubric.criterion: States the bottom-up build's cost as the sum of node heights
rubric.excellent: Explicitly says the sum of all node heights in a complete tree is O(n), and that most nodes are near the bottom so they sift down only a little.
rubric.acceptable: Mentions that most nodes are near the bottom and sift down little, but does not connect to the sum of heights.
rubric.poor: Does not mention the sum of heights or the position of most nodes.

rubric.criterion: States the per-insert cost and the total for n inserts
rubric.excellent: Says each insert can sift up O(log n) levels, so n inserts cost O(n log n) in the worst case.
rubric.acceptable: Says each insert is O(log n) but does not multiply by n.
rubric.poor: Does not state the per-insert cost or the total.

rubric.excellent: Explicitly contrasts bottom-up build with repeated inserts and explains why the former avoids the log factor.
rubric.acceptable: Describes both methods but does not explicitly contrast their costs.
rubric.poor: Describes only one method or confuses the two.
